messages.subject: Simple single-year detection and occupancy probability with no covariates
parts:
Hi everyone,

I'm new to unmarked so please bear with the simplicity of this question. I want to model single-year detection AND occupancy probability at 7 sites with 3 visits each. I don't have covariates like habitat type. In method 1, I set "site" as the "Habitat" so that I can see if occupancy is different at each of the sites. However, I don't think this is the way that Habitat in "occu()" is meant to be used. Either way, my predicted occupancy probabilities seem to be wrong as they're identical at all the sites. Also, I want to model detection probability but I want to make sure my set up is right first.

Any advice is appreciated!

-------

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Simple single-year detection and occupancy probability with no covariates
parts:
hi Joanna,
 
 All 7 of your sites are observed to be occupied and hence the estimated occupancy rate is psi = 1 for all habitat types (there is small numerical error making it < 1 just a little).  So there is no observed variation in occupancy in your sample, and hence it is pointless to model occupancy with this data set.
 Moreover, with a categorical habitat "type" variable having 7 levels (as in your case) this is 7 parameters in the occupancy model. As a rule of thumb I would suggest having 10-20 sites per occupancy parameter in your model. So I think you need at least 70 to think about fitting this model  (this is my own personal rule of thumb not one that I will defend).
 
regards,
andy

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Simple single-year detection and occupancy probability with no covariates
parts:
Dear Joanna,

do you mean you want to model detection probability when occupancy is equal to 1 ? Yes, in that case you could simply use a logistic regression by function glm() in R (although using occu() in unmarked would not be wrong).

An occupancy model is the combination of two logistic regressions and looks like this:
z_i ~ Bernoulli(psi)                # presence/absence z at a site as a function of occupancy prob. psi
y_ij ~ Bernoulli(z_i * p_ij)       # detection or nondetection y an an occupied site as a function of presence/absence z and detection prob. p

When the parameter of either of the two logistic regressions is equal to 1, you are back to a simple logistic regression.

Note however that Andy's caveat about sample size applies: with only 7 sites, you have very little leeway to model structure in your data (i.e., throw in covariates).

Kind regards  --  Marc
